result.determinismNotes:
ORDERING / FP-CRITICAL FACTS

1. Index space. The C++ port does NOT divide by `dim` like earcut.js. `Earcut<N>::vertices` is a running counter reset to 0 in `operator()`; `linkedList()` assigns `insertNode(vertices + i, points[i], last)` and then does `vertices += len;` AFTER the ring is linked. So ring 0 gets indices [0, n0), ring 1 gets [n0, n0+n1), etc. — exactly "the flattened concatenation of all rings".

2. `len` is deliberately UNDER-counted. The accumulation loop is `for (i = 0; threshold >= 0 && i < points.size(); i++) { threshold -= (int)points[i].size(); len += points[i].size(); }`. The `threshold >= 0` guard is evaluated BEFORE each iteration, so once threshold goes negative the loop stops and later rings are not added to `len`. `len` is used only for `nodes.reset(len * 3 / 2)` and `indices.reserve(len + points[0].size())`, so it does not affect output — but it must be reproduced if you are matching allocation behavior.

3. Hashing predicate is `hashing = threshold < 0`, i.e. z-order hashing is ON iff the total vertex count over all rings is STRICTLY GREATER than 80. Exactly 80 => hashing off.

4. Bounding box is computed AFTER `eliminateHoles`, and by walking the LINKED LIST (`p = outerNode->next; do {...} while (p != outerNode);`), seeded with `minX = maxX = outerNode->x; minY = maxY = outerNode->y;`. This is a genuine divergence from earcut.js, which computes the bbox over the raw outer-ring coordinate slice only. The C++ bbox therefore INCLUDES hole vertices (and revisits bridge-duplicated vertices). This changes `inv_size`, hence `zOrder()` values, hence the isEarHashed scan order, hence potentially the emitted triangles, for polygons with holes and >80 vertices. Do not "fix" it.

5. `inv_size = std::max<double>(maxX - minX, maxY - minY); inv_size = inv_size != .0 ? (32767. / inv_size) : .0;` — two statements, reusing the same variable. Do not fuse into one expression; the intermediate is a double rounding of the extent.

6. `area(p,q,r)` must stay literally `(q->y - p->y) * (r->x - q->x) - (q->x - p->x) * (r->y - q->y)`. Every reflex test is `area(a,b,c) >= 0` → reject (note `>=`, so exactly-collinear/zero-area corners are NOT ears). The inner containment test is `pointInTriangle(...) && area(p->prev, p, p->next) >= 0` — again `>=`, and the two conjuncts are short-circuited in that order (pointInTriangle first).

7. Triangle emission order in `earcutLinked` is always three consecutive `indices.emplace_back(...)` in the order prev->i, ear->i, next->i. In `cureLocalIntersections` it is a->i, p->i, b->i where a = p->prev and b = p->next->next (i.e. the node p->next is skipped and both p and p->next are removed).

8. After clipping an ear, BOTH `ear` and `stop` are set to `next->next` (skip one vertex), then `continue` — the `while (ear->prev != ear->next)` condition is re-tested. This "skip next vertex" is the single biggest determinant of output ordering.

9. The `if (ear == stop)` block always ends in `break`, regardless of which pass branch ran. The recursive calls happen before the break; the outer loop never resumes.

10. Ring traversal is always via `->next` (forward). `isEar` scans `p = ear->next->next` forward until `p == ear->prev`. `cureLocalIntersections` scans forward with `do { ... p = p->next; } while (p != start)`. `splitEarcut`'s outer loop advances `a = a->next` forward, inner loop `b = a->next->next` forward until `b == a->prev`. First valid diagonal found in that scan order wins, and the function returns immediately.

11. `splitEarcut` calls `earcutLinked(a)` (the half containing the original `a`) BEFORE `earcutLinked(c)` (the half returned by `splitPolygon`). Both use the default pass = 0, so `indexCurve` may run again on each half if hashing is on.

12. `pass` propagation: pass 0 → `earcutLinked(filterPoints(ear), 1)`. Confirmed: the argument is literally the return value of `filterPoints(ear)` (single-arg form, `end` defaults to nullptr), NOT `ear`. `filterPoints` may return nullptr, which the recursive call handles via `if (!ear) return;`.

13. `indexCurve(ear)` is called only when `!pass && hashing` — i.e. only on pass 0, including the pass-0 calls made from `splitEarcut`.

14. `hashing`, `minX/minY/maxX/maxY`, `inv_size` are Earcut member state, written once per `operator()` call and read by `earcutLinked`/`isEarHashed`/`zOrder`. `hashing` is set unconditionally each call (`hashing = threshold < 0;`), so no stale state leaks between calls, but `minX/minY/inv_size` are only overwritten when hashing is true (stale otherwise — harmless since they are unread then).

15. `std::min<double>` / `std::max<double>` are used with explicit template args in the bbox loop (avoids type-deduction issues); their tie/NaN behavior is std::min/std::max semantics (returns first arg on ties/NaN-left).

16. `nodes` is an arena (`ObjectStore<Node>`); node ADDRESSES are not stable across `nodes.reset()` but pointer identity comparisons (`p != start`, `ear == stop`, `a->i != b->i`) are all that matter. `nodes.clear()` is called at the very end of `operator()`.

functions.name: mapbox::earcut (free function)
functions.signature: template <typename N = uint32_t, typename Polygon> std::vector<N> earcut(const Polygon& poly)
functions.notes: Thin wrapper. Constructs a fresh Earcut<N> per call (so `vertices`, `indices`, `nodes`, `hashing` all start clean), invokes operator(), and moves out the index vector. Polygon is any container-of-containers-of-points; point access goes through mapbox::util::nth<0/1, Point>::get.

functions.name: Earcut<N>::operator()
functions.signature: template <typename N> template <typename Polygon> void Earcut<N>::operator()(const Polygon& points)
functions.notes: Early-outs, in order: (a) `!points.size()` -> return with empty indices; (b) linkedList(points[0], true) returns null, or the outer ring collapsed to <3 distinct nodes (`outerNode->prev == outerNode->next`) -> return. eliminateHoles runs only when there is more than one ring, and it runs BEFORE the bbox pass. `earcutLinked(outerNode)` uses the default pass = 0. `nodes.clear()` releases the arena but `indices` is kept for the caller. Note `hashing` is assigned unconditionally so a previous call cannot leave it set.

functions.name: Earcut<N>::linkedList (context for index numbering)
functions.signature: template <typename N> template <typename Ring> typename Earcut<N>::Node* Earcut<N>::linkedList(const Ring& points, const bool clockwise)
functions.notes: Included because the driver's index semantics depend on it. The emitted `i` values are `vertices + ring-local index`, so they are indices into the flattened concatenation of all rings regardless of whether the ring had to be reversed. The shoelace form `sum += (p20 - p10) * (p11 + p21)` must not be rearranged. `clockwise == (sum > 0)` -> forward insertion; else reverse insertion (`for (i = len; i-- > 0;)`). Outer ring is called with clockwise=true, holes with clockwise=false.

functions.name: Earcut<N>::earcutLinked
functions.signature: template <typename N> void Earcut<N>::earcutLinked(Node* ear, int pass = 0)
functions.notes: CONFIRMED: the pass-0 fallback is literally `earcutLinked(filterPoints(ear), 1)` — filterPoints is applied to the CURRENT ear pointer (which at that moment equals `stop`), and its return value is passed directly; there is no intermediate assignment to `ear`. The pass-1 branch DOES assign (`ear = cureLocalIntersections(filterPoints(ear));`) before recursing with pass 2. Loop condition is `ear->prev != ear->next` (i.e. keep going while at least 3 nodes remain). Note `prev`/`next` are captured BEFORE the ear test, and `next->next` is read AFTER `removeNode(ear)` (removeNode does not touch next->next, so this is equivalent, but reproduce the order). The `stop` sentinel is reset on every successful clip, so the no-progress detection is 'walked a full lap without clipping'. There is NO iteration counter in this function. When `ear == stop` the function always breaks out of the while loop after the ladder; a pass-3+ value (never produced internally) would fall through all branches and just break.

functions.name: Earcut<N>::isEar
functions.signature: template <typename N> bool Earcut<N>::isEar(Node* ear)
functions.notes: Reflex rejection uses `>= 0` (CCW-negative-area convention: after linkedList normalization the working ring has area(a,b,c) < 0 for convex corners). The scan range is exactly the strictly-interior vertices: starts at ear->next->next, stops when it reaches ear->prev, so neither a, b, nor c is tested against its own triangle. The bbox test uses inclusive `>=`/`<=` on all four sides and is a pure conservative pre-filter — it can never flip the result versus the older variant, because pointInTriangle's three cross-product sign tests can only be all-non-negative for a point inside the closed triangle, which is inside the closed bbox. The nested ternaries for x0/y0/x1/y1 use strict `<`/`>` (ties take the later candidate); this is only observable for NaN inputs. The three conjuncts short-circuit left to right: bbox, then pointInTriangle, then the reflex check on p itself (so convex intruding vertices are ignored — only reflex or collinear intruders veto the ear).

functions.name: Earcut<N>::cureLocalIntersections
functions.signature: template <typename N> typename Earcut<N>::Node* Earcut<N>::cureLocalIntersections(Node* start)
functions.notes: Emission order is a->i, p->i, b->i where a = p->prev and b = p->next->next — note that p->next itself is NEVER emitted, it is just deleted. The four guards short-circuit in exactly this order: !equals(a,b), intersects(a,p,p->next,b), locallyInside(a,b), locallyInside(b,a). CRITICAL removal order: `removeNode(p)` runs first, then `removeNode(p->next)`. Because removeNode only rewires neighbours and does not null out p's own next/prev pointers, `p->next` still reads the original successor after the first call — so the second call removes the intended node. Reproduce this literally; do not hoist `Node* pn = p->next;`. On a cure, BOTH `p` and `start` are reassigned to b, and then the unconditional `p = p->next` at the bottom of the loop body immediately advances p to b->next — so the do/while termination test `p != start` compares b->next against b and the loop continues for another full lap from the new anchor. Returns `filterPoints(p)` (single-arg, end = nullptr), not filterPoints(start); at the point of return p == start anyway because the loop exited on that condition.

functions.name: Earcut<N>::splitEarcut
functions.signature: template <typename N> void Earcut<N>::splitEarcut(Node* start)
functions.notes: Outer loop is a do/while over every node starting at `start`, advancing forward; inner loop starts at a->next->next and advances forward until it hits a->prev (exclusive), so adjacent pairs are never considered. Guard order: cheap `a->i != b->i` first (this rejects bridge-duplicated hole vertices that share an index), then the expensive isValidDiagonal(a, b). The FIRST qualifying (a, b) in this scan order is used and the function RETURNS immediately — no further diagonals are tried, and no attempt is made if the whole double loop finds nothing (silent give-up, those vertices are simply never triangulated). splitPolygon(a, b) returns the new node `c` (the b-side copy) and rewires so that `a` anchors one loop and `c` the other. Both filterPoints calls use the TWO-argument form `filterPoints(x, x->next)`, which walks from x with end = x->next (i.e. cleans collinear/duplicate points around the fresh cut and returns a surviving anchor, possibly nullptr). Recursion order is a-half then c-half, both with pass defaulting to 0, so indexCurve re-runs on each half when hashing is enabled.

functions.name: Earcut<N>::area / pointInTriangle (exact FP forms used by isEar)
functions.signature: double area(const Node* p, const Node* q, const Node* r) const;  bool pointInTriangle(double ax, double ay, double bx, double by, double cx, double cy, double px, double py) const;
functions.notes: These are the exact expression forms; any algebraic rearrangement (e.g. expanding products, or moving a term across the >=) changes rounding and can flip a sign at near-degenerate corners, which changes which vertex is clipped and therefore the whole triangle sequence. The three pointInTriangle conjuncts are in the order (c,a), (a,b), (b,c) and short-circuit; all use `>= 0`, so boundary points count as inside. `equals` is exact double comparison, no epsilon. Note earcut 3.x refactored pointInTriangle to the `lhs >= rhs` two-product form; the 2.x C++ port uses the subtract-then-compare-to-zero form shown here.

result.determinismNotes:
GENERAL

- All z values are `int32_t` (member `Node::z`, default-initialized to `0`). All coordinates are `double`. `inv_size`, `minX`, `minY`, `maxX`, `maxY` are `double` members of the `Earcut<N>` functor; `hashing` is a `bool` member.
- earcut.hpp uses the RECIPROCAL form: `inv_size = 32767. / (max span)`, and zOrder MULTIPLIES by it. It does NOT divide by a `size`. (Old earcut 2.0.x JS used `x = 32767 * (x - minX) / size;` — the C++ port and modern JS both use the multiply-by-invSize form. Using the divide form gives bit-different results for some inputs because `(a-b)*(32767/s)` != `32767*(a-b)/s` in IEEE754, and the truncating cast can then land on a different integer, changing z, changing sort order, changing emitted triangle order. This must be reproduced exactly.)
- The cast is a C-style/`static_cast<int32_t>` truncation toward zero, equivalent to JS `| 0`. Inputs are always >= 0 because minX/minY come from a full scan of the same node set, so truncation == floor here, but write it as a truncating cast anyway.
- Degenerate case: if `maxX-minX` and `maxY-minY` are both 0, `inv_size` is set to `.0` (not inf). Then every z is 0 and the sort is a stable no-op. `hashing` is still true.
- Bit-interleave arithmetic never overflows: inputs are in [0, 32767] (15 bits), spread to bits 0,2,...,28; `y << 1` occupies bits 1,3,...,29. Result fits in int32 positive range. No UB from the `<< 8` etc. since values stay under 2^30.

ORDERING / OBSERVABILITY

- `sortLinked` is a bottom-up (Simon Tatham) merge sort and is STABLE via `p->z <= q->z` (take from the left/`p` run on ties). Using `<` instead would swap equal-z nodes and change which candidate `isEarHashed` encounters first — but more importantly it changes nothing about correctness while changing nothing observable *unless* the walk terminates early; still, reproduce `<=` exactly.
- Ties in z are extremely common (all duplicate coordinates, and any two points that quantize into the same 15x15-bit cell), so stability is load-bearing for byte-identical output in practice.
- The initial order fed to `sortLinked` is the ring order starting at `start` (the node `indexCurve` was called with), broken between `start->prev` and `start`. So the pre-sort sequence is start, start->next, ..., start->prev. Changing which node `earcutLinked` was entered at changes the pre-sort permutation and therefore the post-sort order of equal-z nodes.
- `indexCurve` DISCARDS the head returned by `sortLinked`. Nothing ever traverses from the head; all traversal starts at `ear->prevZ` / `ear->nextZ`. Do not "fix" this.
- `isEarHashed` short-circuits on the FIRST blocking candidate found. The order of the two halves of the simultaneous loop body (p-side checked and advanced first, then n-side) is observable only via performance, not result — but the loop's *termination condition* (`p && p->z >= minZ && n && n->z <= maxZ`, all four ANDed) is observable, because it decides which of the two tail loops runs and how far.
- `area(...) >= 0` (not `>`) both as the reflex test and as the candidate-is-reflex test. `pointInTriangle` uses three `>= 0` tests. Do not change any to `>`.
- Keep the cross-product expression forms verbatim: `area(p,q,r) = (q->y - p->y) * (r->x - q->x) - (q->x - p->x) * (r->y - q->y)`.

Z-CHAIN MAINTENANCE

- `removeNode(p)` also unlinks p from the z chain (`if (p->prevZ) p->prevZ->nextZ = p->nextZ; if (p->nextZ) p->nextZ->prevZ = p->prevZ;`). Every node removal (ear cut, `filterPoints`, `cureLocalIntersections`) therefore keeps the z chain consistent. Nodes newly created by `splitPolygon` are NOT inserted into the z chain; they get `z == 0`, `prevZ == nextZ == nullptr`, and are only integrated when a later `indexCurve` runs over their ring (i.e. via `splitEarcut` -> `earcutLinked(a)` with pass 0).
- Because `splitEarcut` calls `earcutLinked(a)` / `earcutLinked(c)` with the default `pass = 0`, `indexCurve` runs AGAIN on each half when hashing is on. `p->z = p->z ? p->z : zOrder(p->x, p->y)` means already-computed z values are reused verbatim and only new/zero-z nodes are computed. A node whose true zOrder is exactly 0 (a point at the bbox min corner) is harmlessly recomputed every time. Reproduce the ternary, not an `if (p->z == 0)`.

functions.name: operator() — hashing enablement and bbox / inv_size setup
functions.signature: template <typename Polygon> void Earcut<N>::operator()(const Polygon& points)
functions.notes: HASHING IS ENABLED IFF the total number of input vertices summed over rings exceeds 80 (threshold starts at 80, each ring's size is subtracted while threshold >= 0; hashing = threshold < 0). Exactly 80 total vertices => threshold == 0 => hashing == FALSE. 81 => hashing == TRUE. The bbox scan happens AFTER eliminateHoles, so it walks the single merged ring and therefore covers every hole vertex too (holes were bridged in with duplicated nodes). minX/minY/inv_size are computed once and never recomputed, even after splitEarcut. `inv_size` defaults to 0 as a member; when hashing is false it is never read. Note the doubled `inv_size` assignment: it temporarily holds the span, then is overwritten with the reciprocal — reproduce the `!= .0` guard so a zero-area bbox yields inv_size == 0.0 rather than inf/NaN.

functions.name: zOrder
functions.signature: int32_t Earcut<N>::zOrder(const double x_, const double y_)
functions.notes: MULTIPLY BY inv_size — earcut.hpp stores the reciprocal `inv_size = 32767. / max(maxX-minX, maxY-minY)` and multiplies here. It does NOT store a `size` and divide. The 32767 constant lives in the setup code (operator()), NOT in zOrder; zOrder itself contains no 32767. The cast is a truncation toward zero (equivalent to JS `x = (x - minX) * invSize | 0`). Both axes use the SAME inv_size (isotropic scaling off the larger span), so the shorter axis does not use its full 15 bits. Shift/mask sequence order is 8/0x00FF00FF, 4/0x0F0F0F0F, 2/0x33333333, 1/0x55555555 for each axis independently; x occupies even bits, y is shifted left one into odd bits. Final combine is `x | (y << 1)` — x is the LOW bit of each pair. Intermediate `x << 8` on a 15-bit value cannot overflow int32.

functions.name: indexCurve
functions.signature: void Earcut<N>::indexCurve(Node* start)
functions.notes: The z chain is seeded as an exact copy of the ring order (prevZ=prev, nextZ=next) traversed FORWARD from `start`, then the circle is cut between start->prev and start, making a linear list whose head is `start` and whose tail is `start->prev`. The pre-sort sequence is therefore start, start->next, ..., start->prev — this permutation determines the relative order of equal-z nodes after the stable sort, so the identity of `start` is observable in the final triangle order. `p->z ? p->z : zOrder(...)` reuses any previously computed z (matters on the second and later indexCurve calls triggered by splitEarcut, and for nodes created by splitPolygon which arrive with z == 0). The `sortLinked` return value is dropped; the sorted list is only ever reached through per-node prevZ/nextZ pointers.

functions.name: sortLinked
functions.signature: typename Earcut<N>::Node* Earcut<N>::sortLinked(Node* list)
functions.notes: Bottom-up merge sort over the nextZ/prevZ chain, in place, no allocation. Key exactness points: (1) the pSize counting loop runs `inSize` times but breaks early when q hits null — pSize ends as the ACTUAL length of the left run; (2) qSize is optimistically set to inSize and is bounds-checked by the `!q` / `qSize > 0 && q` conditions; (3) the branch cascade order is exactly: pSize==0 -> take q; qSize==0 || !q -> take p; p->z <= q->z -> take p; else take q. The `<=` makes the sort STABLE (equal z keeps original relative order) and is directly observable in output for polygons with duplicate/co-cell points; (4) prevZ is rewired on every emitted element (`e->prevZ = tail`) so the result is a correct doubly-linked list; (5) `tail->nextZ = nullptr` after each pass is an UNGUARDED dereference — safe only because sortLinked is never called with an empty list (indexCurve always passes a non-null ring); (6) termination is `numMerges <= 1` checked AFTER the tail fixup and BEFORE doubling inSize, so the final pass's list is returned; (7) `inSize *= 2` at the bottom of the outer loop. The returned head is discarded by the only caller.

functions.name: isEarHashed
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::isEarHashed(Node* ear)
functions.notes:
STRUCTURE: one simultaneous bidirectional loop whose guard is the 4-way conjunction `p && p->z >= minZ && n && n->z <= maxZ` (so it stops as soon as EITHER direction is exhausted), followed by two single-direction tail loops that drain whichever side still has range left. The p-side always uses `>= minZ` and walks prevZ; the n-side always uses `<= maxZ` and walks nextZ. Both bounds are INCLUSIVE.

GUARDS: the bbox-containment pre-check (`p->x >= minTX && p->x <= maxTX && p->y >= minTY && p->y <= maxTY`) is a pure fast-reject and is semantically redundant with pointInTriangle — it changes no results, only speed. VERSION DIFFERENCE: in the modern source (earcut 2.2.3+/2.2.4, matching earcut.hpp master) the bbox pre-check is present in ALL THREE loops. In the simultaneous loop it is written FIRST (before the identity checks) and the identity checks are written as `p !== a && p !== c`; in the two tail loops the identity checks come FIRST and are written as `p !== ear.prev && p !== ear.next`. `a == ear->prev` and `c == ear->next` so the two spellings are identical in effect. In OLDER versions (earcut <= 2.1.x, earcut.hpp <= ~0.12) there is NO simultaneous loop at all: it is two sequential loops, first `p = ear->nextZ; while (p && p->z <= maxZ)` then `p = ear->prevZ; while (p && p->z >= minZ)`, each with only `p != ear->prev && p != ear->next && pointInTriangle(...) && area(p->prev,p,p->next) >= 0` and NO bbox pre-check. The old and new forms return the same boolean, so triangle output is identical; only the traversal cost differs.

Note the ear node itself is never a false positive: `p`/`n` start one step away in the z chain, and `ear` cannot be its own prevZ/nextZ. But `ear` CAN be revisited? No — the z chain is linear (not circular), so each walk terminates at null.

pointInTriangle(ax,ay,bx,by,cx,cy,px,py) == ((cx-px)*(ay-py) - (ax-px)*(cy-py) >= 0) && ((ax-px)*(by-py) - (bx-px)*(ay-py) >= 0) && ((bx-px)*(cy-py) - (cx-px)*(by-py) >= 0). Keep all three as >= 0 and in that operand order.

MIN/MAX NESTING: reproduce `std::min<double>(a->x, std::min<double>(b->x, c->x))` exactly (inner pair is b,c). With NaN-free inputs this matches Math.min(ax,bx,cx); with NaNs it does not, but earcut is undefined on NaN input anyway.

functions.signature: void Earcut<N>::earcutLinked(Node* ear, int pass = 0)

result.subsystem: mapbox/earcut.hpp — ring construction (linkedList/insertNode/removeNode) and hole elimination (eliminateHoles / eliminateHole / findHoleBridge / sectorContainsSector / getLeftmost / splitPolygon), plus the helpers they call (filterPoints, equals, area, pointInTriangle, locallyInside). Primary target = earcut.hpp v2.2.3/v2.2.4 ("newer"); the v2.1.x ("older") variants are given in full alongside.

functions.name: operator() — call-site context for this subsystem
functions.signature: template <typename Polygon> void Earcut<N>::operator()(const Polygon& points)
functions.notes:
IMPORTANT ORDERING FACTS FOR REPRODUCTION:
(1) `vertices` is a member counter, reset to 0 at the top of operator(), and advanced by `vertices += len` at the END of each linkedList() call. So ring r's node i gets index (sum of sizes of rings 0..r-1) + i, i.e. exactly the flattened-input index, EVEN WHEN the ring is inserted in reverse.
(2) Rings are built in order 0,1,2,...,k: outer first (inside operator()), then holes 1..k-1 inside eliminateHoles' queue-building loop, in ascending ring order — the sort happens AFTER all holes are linked, so node indices are unaffected by the sort.
(3) The guard `outerNode->prev == outerNode->next` (degenerate <=2-node outer ring) is a 2.2.x addition; earcut.hpp 2.1.x had only `if (!outerNode) return;`.
(4) `threshold` starts at 80 and the loop condition is `threshold >= 0 && i < points.size()` — note len is therefore only a partial sum when there are many points; this only affects the arena size hint and reserve(), not output.
Node struct fields relevant here: const N i; const double x, y; Node *prev, *next; int32_t z = 0; Node *prevZ = nullptr, *nextZ = nullptr; bool steiner = false;

functions.name: linkedList
functions.signature: template <typename Ring> Node* Earcut<N>::linkedList(const Ring& points, const bool clockwise)
functions.notes:
* j TRAILS i: the loop is `for (i = 0, j = len-1; i < len; j = i++)`, so on iteration i, j == (i + len - 1) % len, i.e. p1 = points[i] is the CURRENT point and p2 = points[j] is the PREVIOUS point. The very first iteration pairs points[0] with points[len-1]. Accumulation order is i = 0,1,2,...,len-1 — do not reorder, double addition is not associative.
* The expression is literally `(p2.x - p1.x) * (p1.y + p2.y)` with p2 = previous, p1 = current. Do NOT rewrite as the usual shoelace form.
* `len > 0 ? len - 1 : 0` guards the unsigned underflow for an empty ring; the loop body then never runs.
* `clockwise == (sum > 0)`: strict `>` — sum == 0 (degenerate/zero-area ring) counts as NOT clockwise, so a zero-area ring is emitted FORWARD when clockwise==false (holes) and REVERSED when clockwise==true (outer ring).
* Reverse loop is `for (i = len; i-- > 0;)`, i.e. i takes len-1, len-2, ..., 0. Insertion is still `insertNode(vertices + i, ...)`, so INDEX ASSIGNMENT IS BY POSITION IN THE INPUT RING, not by insertion order. `last` after the loop points at the last-inserted node = points[0] in the reverse case, points[len-1] in the forward case.
* insertNode appends AFTER `last` and returns the new node, so the returned `last` is the final node of the ring and `last->next` is the first-inserted node.
* Trailing dedup: `if (last && equals(last, last->next)) { removeNode(last); last = last->next; }` — this removes exactly ONE duplicate, the closing vertex of a ring whose first == last point. It compares the final inserted node against the FIRST inserted node. Present in all earcut.hpp 2.x (added upstream in earcut.js 2.1.2). Note `vertices += len` still adds the FULL len, so index alignment with the flat input is preserved even though a node was dropped.
* linkedList is called as linkedList(points[0], true) for the outer ring and linkedList(points[i], false) for holes.

functions.name: insertNode
functions.signature: template <typename Point> Node* Earcut<N>::insertNode(std::size_t i, const Point& pt, Node* last)
functions.notes: Inserts p immediately AFTER `last` in the circular list, so successive calls build the ring in the order given. `nodes` is an arena (ObjectStore); node identity/pointer ordering is allocation-ordered, which matters only if you ever tie-break on pointers (earcut never does). The stored index is `static_cast<N>(i)` — N is typically uint32_t.

functions.name: removeNode
functions.signature: void Earcut<N>::removeNode(Node* p)
functions.notes: Nodes are never freed (arena). p's own prev/next are left dangling-but-valid, which filterPoints relies on (`p = end = p->prev` after removeNode(p)).

functions.name: eliminateHoles
functions.signature: template <typename Polygon> Node* Earcut<N>::eliminateHoles(const Polygon& points, Node* outerNode)
functions.notes:
* Ring loop is ASCENDING i = 1..len-1, so hole nodes get ascending index blocks regardless of the later sort.
* `if (list)` guard is C++-only (an empty hole ring makes linkedList return nullptr; earcut.js would throw). A hole contributing nullptr is silently skipped BUT `vertices` was still advanced by its len inside linkedList, so indices stay aligned.
* `if (list == list->next) list->steiner = true;` marks a degenerate 1-node ring so that filterPoints will never delete it. Note this tests the node RETURNED by linkedList; a 2-point ring whose points are equal also collapses to 1 node via the trailing dedup and therefore also gets steiner=true.
* getLeftmost(list) is what goes into the queue — NOT `list`.
* !!! std::sort IS NOT STABLE (libstdc++/libc++ use introsort: median-of-3 quicksort -> heapsort at depth 2*log2(n) -> final insertion sort with a 16-element threshold). The comparator is strict-weak on x only, so TWO OR MORE HOLES WITH EQUAL LEFTMOST x ARE ORDERED IMPLEMENTATION-DEFINED-LY. Their relative order changes which hole gets bridged first, which changes the bridge choices for the rest, which changes the emitted triangle order. For byte-identical output you must reproduce the SAME std::sort implementation (or precompute the permutation on a reference build). This is also a genuine earcut.hpp-vs-earcut.js divergence: JS `Array.prototype.sort` is spec-stable since ES2019, so JS keeps ascending-ring order for x-ties.
* Upstream earcut.js 3.x replaced the comparator with `compareXYSlope` (x, then y, then slope (next.y-y)/(next.x-x)). earcut.hpp 2.2.4 does NOT have this — it is plain `a->x < b->x`.
* Variant (A) is used by earcut.hpp 2.2.0+ (and earcut.js 2.2.0+). Variant (B) is used by earcut.hpp 2.1.x and earlier (and earcut.js 2.1.x and earlier). The two are NOT equivalent: (B) re-filters the ORIGINAL outerNode chain after every hole (and can therefore return a node that (A) would never land on), while (A) lets eliminateHole choose the new anchor. Under (B), outerNode is also passed BY VALUE into eliminateHole, so the caller's outerNode is untouched by findHoleBridge's reassignment inside the callee.

functions.name: eliminateHole
functions.signature: NEWER: Node* Earcut<N>::eliminateHole(Node* hole, Node* outerNode)   |   OLDER: void Earcut<N>::eliminateHole(Node* hole, Node* outerNode)
functions.notes:
* ORDER OF THE TWO filterPoints CALLS DIFFERS BETWEEN V2 AND V3 (V2 filters `bridge` first then `bridgeReverse`; V3 filters `bridgeReverse` first then `bridge`). filterPoints mutates the shared ring, so the order is observable when the two cut neighbourhoods overlap (e.g. when the bridge endpoints are adjacent or the hole is a single Steiner vertex).
* V1 calls filterPoints ONLY on b (== the splitPolygon return, i.e. b2), never on the bridge side inside eliminateHole; the bridge side is cleaned by the caller's `filterPoints(outerNode, outerNode->next)` — and note that in V1 the caller's `outerNode` is the ORIGINAL outer anchor, not the bridge, because the reassignment inside eliminateHole is to a by-value parameter.
* The comment "Check if input node was removed by the filtering" is vestigial in V3 (it belonged to V2's ternary); its presence is a reliable fingerprint of the 2.2.3+ file.
* V3 can return a node belonging to the merged ring at/near the bridge, so the anchor WALKS as holes are consumed — this feeds directly into the next hole's findHoleBridge starting point `p = outerNode`, and findHoleBridge's do/while traversal order (p = p->next from that anchor) determines which of several equal-qx segments wins the `x > qx` strict comparison. Getting the anchor wrong changes output.
* splitPolygon(bridge, hole): argument order matters — a = bridge (outer ring node), b = hole (the hole's leftmost node).

functions.name: findHoleBridge
functions.signature: Node* Earcut<N>::findHoleBridge(Node* hole, Node* outerNode)
functions.notes:
EVERY DETAIL BELOW IS LOAD-BEARING.

FIRST LOOP (leftward ray scan):
* Traversal is FORWARD from outerNode (`p = p->next`), do/while, terminating when p == outerNode again. The first node tested is outerNode itself.
* Condition is `hy <= p->y && hy >= p->next->y && p->next->y != p->y` — asymmetric: <= on the from-endpoint, >= on the to-endpoint. Only DOWNWARD-going edges (p->y >= hy >= p->next->y) are considered. The `p->next->y != p->y` test excludes horizontal edges AND makes the division safe.
* x interpolation, EXACT FORM (multiply before divide, left-to-right): `p->x + (hy - p->y) * (p->next->x - p->x) / (p->next->y - p->y)`. Do not factor, do not precompute a reciprocal.
* Acceptance: `x <= hx && x > qx` — NON-strict on hx, STRICT on qx. Strict `> qx` means the FIRST segment achieving a given qx wins; later segments producing the identical x are rejected. Hence the traversal start (outerNode) is observable.
* `m = p->x < p->next->x ? p : p->next;` — STRICT `<`; on a tie (vertical edge) it picks p->next.
* `if (x == hx) return m;` EARLY RETURN — NEWER ONLY (2.2.0+). It sits INSIDE the `x <= hx && x > qx` block, AFTER `qx = x` and AFTER `m` is assigned. Flag: the older code instead did the `hy == p->y -> return p / hy == p->next->y -> return p->next` pair BEFORE assigning m, and then, after the loop, `if (hx == qx) return m->prev;` (note: m->PREV, not m — a frequent source of divergence; some 2.2.0/2.2.1 intermediates have `if (hx == qx) return m;`).
* Failure: `if (!m) return 0;` (nullptr).

SECOND LOOP (minimum-tangent selection):
* `stop`, `mx`, `my` are SNAPSHOT from the initial m and are NEVER updated when m is reassigned. So the `p->x >= mx` filter and the pointInTriangle vertices stay pinned to the ORIGINAL m for the whole loop, while the tie-break compares against the CURRENT m (`p->x > m->x`). This asymmetry is intentional in upstream; do not "fix" it.
* NEWER: `p = m;` + do/while, so the very first iteration evaluates p == m itself; hx >= mx && mx >= mx && hx != mx holds (given hx != mx), pointInTriangle is degenerate-but-true for the vertex itself, so tanMin is typically seeded from m on iteration 0. OLDER: `p = m->next;` + while, so m is never evaluated and tanMin can remain +inf. This changes which candidate wins ties.
* Gate `hx >= p->x && p->x >= mx && hx != p->x`: non-strict on both bounds plus an explicit `hx != p->x` (so effectively hx > p->x, guaranteeing a positive denominator in the tan formula).
* pointInTriangle ARGUMENT SWAP, exactly: `pointInTriangle(hy < my ? hx : qx, hy,   mx, my,   hy < my ? qx : hx, hy,   p->x, p->y)`. Vertex A = (hy<my ? hx : qx, hy), Vertex B = (mx, my), Vertex C = (hy<my ? qx : hx, hy), point P = (p->x, p->y). The swap keeps the triangle wound consistently for pointInTriangle's three `>= 0` half-plane tests depending on whether the hole vertex is above or below m. Note the comparison is `hy < my` (strict); hy == my takes the else branch (A = qx, C = hx).
* `double tan = std::abs(hy - p->y) / (hx - p->x);` — std::abs on the numerator only; the denominator is positive by the gate. Keep this exact form (abs of a difference, then divide).
* NEWER short-circuit ORDER: `locallyInside(p, hole) && (tan < tanMin || (tan == tanMin && (p->x > m->x || sectorContainsSector(m, p))))`. locallyInside is evaluated FIRST. OLDER order is the reverse: `(tan < tanMin || (tan == tanMin && p->x > m->x)) && locallyInside(p, hole)`. Both are side-effect-free so only cost differs — but the PREDICATE differs: newer adds `|| sectorContainsSector(m, p)` as an additional way to win an exact tan tie even when p->x <= m->x.
* DIVERGENCE TO FLAG: upstream earcut.js writes the tie-break as `(p.x > m.x || (p.x === m.x && sectorContainsSector(m, p)))`, i.e. the sector test is gated on p.x === m.x. earcut.hpp 2.2.4 (per my recollection, and per the form you quoted) drops the `p->x == m->x &&` guard, so sectorContainsSector can fire when p->x < m->x. If you are matching the C++ byte-for-byte, use the UNGUARDED form; if matching JS, add the guard. See uncertainties.
* `tan == tanMin` is an exact double equality — reachable in practice (collinear ray candidates), so it must be an exact `==`, not an epsilon compare.
* Loop terminates on `p != stop` where stop is the ORIGINAL m, so exactly one full revolution of the merged outer ring.

functions.name: sectorContainsSector
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::sectorContainsSector(const Node* m, const Node* p)
functions.pseudocode:
// whether sector in vertex m contains sector in vertex p in the same coordinates
return area(m->prev, m, p->prev) < 0 && area(p->next, m, m->next) < 0;
functions.notes:
* Added in 2.2.0; absent from 2.1.x entirely — if you are targeting 2.1.x, do not emit this function and use the older tie-break.
* Argument order is asymmetric and must be copied exactly: first term is (m->prev, m, p->prev); second is (p->next, m, m->next). Note m appears as the MIDDLE vertex in both.
* Both comparisons are STRICT `< 0`, and `&&` short-circuits (first term evaluated first).
* area(p,q,r) = (q->y - p->y) * (r->x - q->x) - (q->x - p->x) * (r->y - q->y) — keep verbatim.

functions.name: getLeftmost
functions.signature: Node* Earcut<N>::getLeftmost(Node* start)
functions.notes:
* Traversal is FORWARD from `start` (which is whatever linkedList returned — the LAST-inserted node of the ring, i.e. points[len-1] for forward insertion or points[0] for reversed insertion, possibly shifted by the trailing-duplicate removal). The do/while tests `start` first, and `leftmost` is initialised to `start`, so the first iteration is a no-op self-compare.
* Both comparisons are STRICT `<`. Because of the strictness plus forward traversal, an exact (x,y) duplicate loses to the EARLIER-VISITED node — i.e. the winner is the first node in forward-from-start order achieving the minimum (x, then y) key.
* THE Y TIE-BREAK `|| (p->x == leftmost->x && p->y < leftmost->y)` IS A 2.2.0 ADDITION. earcut.hpp 2.1.x has only `if (p->x < leftmost->x) leftmost = p;` — which on an x-tie keeps the FIRST such node instead of the lowest-y one. This changes the queue entry, hence the bridge, hence everything downstream.
* Note the key is (min x, then min y) — lowest y wins, not highest.

functions.name: splitPolygon
functions.signature: Node* Earcut<N>::splitPolygon(Node* a, Node* b)
functions.notes:
* Allocation order is a2 THEN b2 — matters only for arena layout, not semantics, but keep it if you are diffing arena state.
* a2 and b2 are DUPLICATE nodes: they copy a->i / b->i (so two nodes can carry the same vertex index — this is how a bridge produces repeated indices in the output triangle list) and the exact x/y doubles. Their z / prevZ / nextZ / steiner start at the defaults (0 / nullptr / nullptr / false) — in particular a2/b2 are NOT steiner even if a/b were, and they are NOT in the z-order list.
* `an` and `bp` are captured BEFORE any relinking; the six assignments must happen in the order shown (they are order-sensitive because a->next is overwritten before a2->next = an would otherwise read it).
* Resulting topology: ring1 = ... -> a -> b -> (b's forward chain) -> bp -> b2 -> a2 -> an -> ... (back to a). When a is on the outer ring and b is a hole node, this MERGES them into one ring, and b2 is the node on the "return" side of the bridge.
* RETURNS b2 (not a2, not b). eliminateHole names this `bridgeReverse` (2.2.x) or `b` (2.1.x).

functions.name: filterPoints (helper — called by eliminateHole/eliminateHoles)
functions.signature: Node* Earcut<N>::filterPoints(Node* start, Node* end = nullptr)
functions.notes:
* Forward traversal; on removal it BACKS UP (`p = end = p->prev`) and sets `again` so the loop re-tests the predecessor even if p == end.
* `area(...) == 0` is exact double equality (collinearity), `equals` is exact x&&y equality.
* `steiner` nodes are immune — this is why eliminateHoles sets steiner=true on 1-node holes.
* Returns `end`, which is the last surviving node examined. eliminateHole (V3) RETURNS this value as the new outer anchor, so filterPoints' exact stopping node is part of the observable state.

functions.name: equals / area / pointInTriangle / locallyInside (helpers used by this subsystem)
functions.signature: bool equals(const Node*, const Node*); double area(const Node*, const Node*, const Node*) const; bool pointInTriangle(double,double,double,double,double,double,double,double) const; bool locallyInside(const Node*, const Node*)
functions.notes:
* area MUST stay literally `(q->y - p->y) * (r->x - q->x) - (q->x - p->x) * (r->y - q->y)`. Any algebraic rearrangement changes the sign at near-degenerate configurations and therefore changes triangle emission.
* pointInTriangle: three tests, ALL `>= 0` (boundary counts as inside), evaluated in the listed order with && short-circuit; each is (X - px)*(Y - py) - (X' - px)*(Y' - py). Note the earcut.js 3.x variant flips these to `<= 0` together with a winding change — do not mix.
* locallyInside: the convex branch uses `>= 0 && >= 0`; the reflex branch uses `< 0 || < 0`. The discriminant is STRICT `< 0` (collinear a goes to the reflex branch). In findHoleBridge it is always called as locallyInside(p, hole) — p is the outer-ring candidate, hole is the hole's leftmost node.

result.determinismNotes:
ORDERING / FP HAZARDS, most-to-least dangerous:

1. std::sort in eliminateHoles is NOT STABLE and the comparator only orders on x. Any two holes whose leftmost vertices share an x are permuted implementation-defined-ly (libstdc++ and libc++ both use introsort: median-of-3 quicksort, heapsort fallback at depth 2*floor(log2(n)), final insertion sort with threshold 16 — but their partition details differ, and MSVC differs again). Since eliminateHole is sequential and each hole mutates the ring the next one bridges into, an x-tie permutation changes the entire downstream triangle sequence. If you need byte-identical output against a specific binary, either (a) port that binary's std::sort verbatim, or (b) verify no x-ties exist in your inputs. Upstream earcut.js uses a stable sort here, so JS and C++ can legitimately disagree on x-ties.

2. eliminateHoles/eliminateHole variant choice (A/V3 vs B/V1) changes the outer anchor that findHoleBridge starts scanning from, and findHoleBridge's `x > qx` is STRICT — so among segments yielding the identical intersection x, the one reached FIRST in forward order from that anchor wins. Anchor identity is therefore observable, not just the ring contents.

3. Node index assignment: `insertNode(vertices + i, points[i], last)` with i = the position in the ring even in the reverse loop, and `vertices += len` at the end of linkedList regardless of whether the trailing duplicate node was removed. This is what keeps output indices equal to flattened-input offsets. Rings with zero points still advance nothing (len == 0) but return nullptr, and the C++ `if (list)` guard silently skips them.

4. Floating-point expression forms that must be copied character-for-character (all are double, no FMA, no reassociation — compile with -fno-fast-math / -ffp-contract=off, and beware x87 excess precision on 32-bit x86: build with SSE2):
   - signed area accumulation: `sum += (p2.x - p1.x) * (p1.y + p2.y)` accumulated for i = 0..len-1 with j trailing i. Order-dependent.
   - ray intersection: `p->x + (hy - p->y) * (p->next->x - p->x) / (p->next->y - p->y)` — multiply first, then divide, then add p->x.
   - tangent: `std::abs(hy - p->y) / (hx - p->x)`.
   - triangle area: `(q->y - p->y) * (r->x - q->x) - (q->x - p->x) * (r->y - q->y)`.
   - pointInTriangle's three cross products in the given operand order.

5. Exact comparison operators that are load-bearing (non-exhaustive but complete for this subsystem):
   - linkedList: `clockwise == (sum > 0)` (strict >, so sum == 0 behaves as counter-clockwise).
   - linkedList trailing dedup: `last && equals(last, last->next)`.
   - findHoleBridge loop 1: `hy <= p->y && hy >= p->next->y && p->next->y != p->y`; `x <= hx && x > qx`; `p->x < p->next->x ? p : p->next`; `x == hx`.
   - findHoleBridge loop 2: `hx >= p->x && p->x >= mx && hx != p->x`; `tan < tanMin`; `tan == tanMin`; `p->x > m->x`; `hy < my` for the pointInTriangle argument swap.
   - getLeftmost: `p->x < leftmost->x || (p->x == leftmost->x && p->y < leftmost->y)`.
   - sectorContainsSector: both terms strict `< 0`.
   - filterPoints: `area(...) == 0` exact.
   - pointInTriangle: all three `>= 0`.
   - locallyInside: discriminant `< 0`; convex branch `>= 0 && >= 0`; reflex branch `< 0 || < 0`.

6. Snapshot-vs-live aliasing in findHoleBridge's second loop: `stop`, `mx`, `my`, and `qx` are frozen from the initial m/first-loop result while `m` itself is reassigned. The gate uses frozen mx, the tie-break uses live m->x. Replicating only one of these produces different bridges.

7. Short-circuit evaluation order in the tan tie-break differs between 2.1.x (`(tan…) && locallyInside(...)`) and 2.2.x (`locallyInside(...) && (tan…)`). Semantically identical (both pure), but preserve it if you are diffing call traces.

8. `qx` initialises to -infinity and `tanMin` to +infinity (std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity()), not to a large finite sentinel.

9. splitPolygon creates two NEW nodes duplicating a->i and b->i, so the same vertex index legitimately appears multiple times in the output triangle list; the duplicates start with steiner=false, z=0, prevZ/nextZ=nullptr regardless of the originals.

result.determinismNotes:
Things that must be preserved byte-for-byte to reproduce identical triangle output:

1. area() expression form: `(q->y - p->y) * (r->x - q->x) - (q->x - p->x) * (r->y - q->y)`. Any algebraic rearrangement (e.g. the more common (b-a)x(c-a) form) changes both the sign convention and the last-bit rounding, and area()==0 / area()>0 tests appear in filterPoints, isValidDiagonal, locallyInside, isEar and the hole-bridge code, so a 1-ulp difference flips triangulations on collinear-ish data.

2. Sign convention is inverted relative to the usual math convention: negative area == convex/CCW. Every `< 0` / `>= 0` / `> 0` in locallyInside, isValidDiagonal, sectorContainsSector, isEar depends on it.

3. pointInTriangle's three products are the SUBTRACTED form compared `>= 0` (2.2.4), not the product-vs-product form of earcut.js 3.0. The two round differently.

4. All coordinates are promoted to double at linkedList time; do not do predicate arithmetic in the input scalar type (e.g. float or int), and do not use long double or FMA. Compile without -ffast-math and without x87 excess precision (-mfpmath=sse on 32-bit x86, or the equivalent), otherwise the exact-zero tests (`area(...) == 0`, `sign()`) misbehave.

5. Traversal directions: intersectsPolygon and middleInside both start AT `a` and walk FORWARD via ->next in a do/while. filterPoints walks forward but rewinds to ->prev on every removal. Reversing any of these changes floating-point accumulation (middleInside) or which edge is found first (intersectsPolygon, cost only) and, for filterPoints, changes the returned node and therefore the start vertex of every downstream loop — which directly reorders emitted triangles.

6. filterPoints' return value IS part of the algorithm's state, not a convenience. `end` advances backwards on removals. Callers assign it back to the ring handle.

7. Index (->i) comparisons, never pointer comparisons, in intersectsPolygon and isValidDiagonal — because splitPolygon manufactures duplicate nodes sharing an index.

8. removeNode leaves the removed node's own pointers intact; other code depends on reading through them afterwards.

9. Short-circuit order in isValidDiagonal and locallyInside affects only cost, not the result — except in the presence of NaN, where the C++ `!= 0` spelling of the sectors clause differs from the JS truthiness spelling.

10. equals() is exact ==; there is no epsilon anywhere in earcut.

functions.name: Node (struct, for reference — field order matters for the surgery routines)
functions.notes: x and y are ALWAYS double, regardless of the coordinate type of the input points (linkedList does util::nth<0,Point>::get(pt) into a double). So all predicate arithmetic is IEEE-754 double even for integer input. `i` is of the output index type N (e.g. uint32_t). Nodes are allocated from an ObjectPool<Node> member named `nodes`; pool identity/addresses are never compared for ordering, only for equality, so allocator behavior does not affect output.
functions.signature: struct Node { Node(N index, double x_, double y_); const N i; const double x; const double y; Node* prev = nullptr; Node* next = nullptr; int32_t z = 0; Node* prevZ = nullptr; Node* nextZ = nullptr; bool steiner = false; };

functions.name: area
functions.notes: DO NOT rearrange. Exactly: (q.y-p.y)*(r.x-q.x) - (q.x-p.x)*(r.y-q.y). Sign convention: this is the NEGATIVE of the usual CCW cross product. For p=(0,0), q=(1,0), r=(0,1) (counter-clockwise in standard math orientation) it returns -1. Hence in earcut a NEGATIVE area means convex/CCW turn, and `area(...) >= 0` means reflex. This is why isEar starts with `if (area(a,b,c) >= 0) return false; // reflex, can't be an ear`, and why signedArea/linkedList orient the outer ring so that traversal yields negative areas. This form and sign convention are IDENTICAL in every version from 0.x through 2.2.4 and in earcut.js 3.0.
functions.signature: double Earcut<N>::area(const Node* p, const Node* q, const Node* r) const

functions.name: equals
functions.notes: Exact double equality (==), both coordinates, x tested first with short-circuit &&. No epsilon anywhere in earcut. It is a plain non-const member function in the header (not marked const), though it reads nothing from `this`. Unchanged across all versions.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::equals(const Node* p1, const Node* p2)

functions.name: pointInTriangle
functions.notes: Three cross products, in this exact order: the (C,A) pair, then (A,B), then (B,C) — i.e. the pairs are cycled C->A, A->B, B->C, and each term is written (Xfirst-px)*(Ysecond-py) - (Xsecond-px)*(Yfirst-py). All three compare `>= 0` (boundary counts as inside). Short-circuit && means later products are not evaluated if an earlier one fails — irrelevant to the result. SIGN CONVENTION: this returns true for a triangle wound the way earcut expects an ear to be wound, i.e. one whose area(a,b,c) is NEGATIVE. Callers always pass (ear->prev, ear, ear->next) as (a,b,c) after already rejecting reflex ears, so the convention is self-consistent. Sanity check: a=(0,0), b=(1,0), c=(0,1) (area = -1) with p=(0.2,0.2) yields +0.2, +0.2, +0.6 — all >= 0, inside. VARIANT: earcut.js 3.0 (2024) rewrote this as three product-vs-product comparisons without the subtraction — `(cx-px)*(ay-py) >= (ax-px)*(cy-py) && (ax-px)*(by-py) >= (bx-px)*(ay-py) && (bx-px)*(cy-py) >= (cx-px)*(by-py)` — and added a companion `pointInTriangleExceptFirst(...)` = `!(ax==px && ay==py) && pointInTriangle(...)` used by isEar/isEarHashed. The C++ port at 2.2.4 has NEITHER; it keeps the subtracted `>= 0` form and has no ExceptFirst helper. The subtracted and product-comparison forms are NOT bit-identical (the subtraction rounds once more), so use the subtracted form for a 2.2.4-faithful port.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::pointInTriangle(double ax, double ay, double bx, double by, double cx, double cy, double px, double py) const

functions.name: sign
functions.notes: Written exactly as the difference of two bool-to-int conversions, with the comparisons in that order: (0.0 < val) minus (val < 0.0). Returns 1 / -1 / 0. NaN yields 0 - 0 = 0. The JS equivalent is `num > 0 ? 1 : num < 0 ? -1 : 0`, same result. Introduced together with the orientation-based `intersects` (earcut.js 2.2.0 / earcut.hpp 2.2.0); it does not exist in 2.1.x and earlier.
functions.signature: int Earcut<N>::sign(double val)

functions.name: onSegment
functions.notes: Bounding-box containment of the MIDDLE argument q inside the box of p and r. Order of the four clauses: x<=max, x>=min, y<=max, y>=min — all inclusive. The explicit `std::max<double>` / `std::min<double>` template argument is in the real source (operands are already double, so it is cosmetic). Only meaningful when the three points are collinear; callers guarantee that. New in 2.2.0.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::onSegment(const Node* p, const Node* q, const Node* r)

functions.name: intersects (current orientation-based version, 2.2.x)
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::intersects(const Node* p1, const Node* q1, const Node* p2, const Node* q2)

functions.name: intersectsPolygon
functions.notes: Traversal starts AT a and walks forward via ->next until it returns to a (do/while, so edge (a, a->next) is the first edge examined and is then skipped by the guard). The guard compares INDICES (->i), not pointers — this matters because splitPolygon duplicates nodes with the same i, so a duplicate vertex node is also excluded. Guard clause order is exactly: p->i != a->i, then p->next->i != a->i, then p->i != b->i, then p->next->i != b->i, then the intersects() call; all joined by && so intersects() is only invoked for edges disjoint (by index) from both diagonal endpoints. Returns on the FIRST hit, so traversal order is observable only through cost, not result. Structure unchanged across versions; only the callee `intersects` changed.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::intersectsPolygon(const Node* a, const Node* b)

functions.name: locallyInside
functions.notes: Branch selector is `area(a->prev, a, a->next) < 0`, i.e. 'a is a CONVEX vertex' under earcut's negated sign convention. Convex branch: BOTH `area(a, b, a->next) >= 0` AND `area(a, a->prev, b) >= 0` — note `>=` (inclusive) and note the operand orders differ between the two calls: (a, b, a->next) vs (a, a->prev, b). Reflex branch: `area(a, b, a->prev) < 0` OR `area(a, a->next, b) < 0` — strict `<`, operand orders (a, b, a->prev) and (a, a->next, b). The asymmetry (>= in the convex branch, < in the reflex branch) is deliberate and load-bearing for degenerate/collinear inputs; do not 'normalize' it. Short-circuit affects cost only. Identical in all versions 2.0.x–2.2.4 and in earcut.js 3.0.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::locallyInside(const Node* a, const Node* b)

functions.name: middleInside
functions.notes: Midpoint computed as (a->x + b->x) / 2 and (a->y + b->y) / 2 — sum then divide by 2, NOT 0.5*(...) (bit-identical here, but keep the form). Classic crossing-number ray cast using strict `<`. Three conditions ANDed in exactly this order: (1) `(p->y > py) != (p->next->y > py)` — strict `>` on both sides, so a vertex exactly at py counts as 'below'; (2) `p->next->y != p->y` — guard added in 2.2.0 to avoid a 0/0 division producing NaN; logically implied by (1) for finite values but present in the source and short-circuiting BEFORE the division, so it changes NaN behavior; (3) `px < (p->next->x - p->x) * (py - p->y) / (p->next->y - p->y) + p->x` — multiply first, then divide, then add p->x; do not re-associate. Toggles `inside` on each crossing. Loop starts at a, walks ->next, do/while until back at a. The result is order-independent in exact arithmetic but not necessarily in floating point, so keep the start-at-a forward walk. OLDER VARIANT (2.1.x and earlier): identical except the `p->next->y != p->y` clause is absent.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::middleInside(const Node* a, const Node* b)

functions.name: isValidDiagonal
functions.notes:
Exact top-level shape: A && B && C && (D || E). The original source relies on && binding tighter than ||, writing a single outer paren pair: `... && !intersectsPolygon(a, b) && (locallyInside(a,b) && locallyInside(b,a) && middleInside(a,b) && (area(...) != 0 || area(...) != 0) || equals(a,b) && area(...) > 0 && area(...) > 0)`. The extra parens in my pseudocode are only for clarity and do not change grouping. Evaluation is left-to-right with short-circuiting; that order is observable via cost only.

Clause by clause:
- `a->next->i != b->i && a->prev->i != b->i` — index comparison, not pointer; b must not be an immediate neighbour of a.
- `!intersectsPolygon(a, b)`.
- locally visible: `locallyInside(a, b) && locallyInside(b, a) && middleInside(a, b)` in that order.
- opposite-facing-sectors clause: `(area(a->prev, a, b->prev) != 0 || area(a, b->prev, b) != 0)`. Note the operand triples: (a->prev, a, b->prev) and (a, b->prev, b) — both involve b->prev, neither involves b->next. C++ writes explicit `!= 0`; earcut.js writes the doubles as truthiness `(area(a.prev, a, b.prev) || area(a, b.prev, b))`. Same semantics except for NaN (NaN != 0 is true in C++, NaN is falsy in JS) — a real if exotic divergence.
- zero-length special case: `equals(a, b) && area(a->prev, a, a->next) > 0 && area(b->prev, b, b->next) > 0`. Note `> 0` (strictly positive = REFLEX under earcut's negated sign convention) at BOTH a and b, using a's own prev/next and b's own prev/next respectively.

OLDER SIMPLER VARIANTS:
- earcut.hpp 2.1.x / earcut.js <= 2.1.5: a flat 6-way AND with no sectors clause and no zero-length clause — `return a->next->i != b->i && a->prev->i != b->i && !intersectsPolygon(a, b) && locallyInside(a, b) && locallyInside(b, a) && middleInside(a, b);`
- Very early (earcut.js 1.x / earcut.hpp 0.9-era): same flat form, with middleInside sometimes taking a separate 'tip' argument or being omitted on the hole-bridging path.
- earcut.js 3.0 (2024): identical to the 2.2.x form above (truthiness spelling for the sectors clause).
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::isValidDiagonal(Node* a, Node* b)

functions.name: sectorContainsSector (adjacent predicate, used by findHoleBridge)
functions.notes: Included because it lives in the same predicate block and is easy to get backwards. Note the asymmetric operand order: the first triple is (m->prev, m, p->prev), the second is (p->next, m, m->next) — m is the MIDDLE argument in both. Both strict `< 0`, joined by &&. Introduced in 2.2.0 to disambiguate hole bridges at coincident x; absent in 2.1.x and earlier.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::sectorContainsSector(const Node* m, const Node* p)

functions.name: filterPoints
functions.notes:
The default argument `end = nullptr` is declared in the class body, not on the out-of-line definition. Semantics point by point:
- `if (!end) end = start;` — the sentinel defaults to the start node.
- Removal test order: `!p->steiner` FIRST (steiner points are never filtered, even if duplicate or collinear), then `equals(p, p->next)` (duplicate of the FOLLOWING node, not the previous), then `area(p->prev, p, p->next) == 0` (exact zero = collinear).
- On removal: `removeNode(p); p = end = p->prev;` — BOTH the cursor and the sentinel move back to the predecessor. This is what lets the loop re-examine the predecessor (which may itself now be collinear) and guarantees the returned node is still linked. Note p->prev is read from the removed node, which removeNode deliberately leaves intact.
- `if (p == p->next) break;` — the ring has collapsed to a single self-linked node; bail out immediately WITHOUT setting `again`. The function still returns `end`, which is that degenerate self-loop node, so callers must tolerate it (earcutLinked's `if (!ear) return;` does not catch it; the ear loop's `ear->prev != ear->next` check does).
- `again = true;` after a successful removal forces at least one more iteration regardless of where p landed relative to end.
- Loop condition `while (again || p != end)` — `again` is checked first.
- RETURNS `end`: the last node that survived a removal, or the original start/end sentinel if nothing was removed. Callers reassign their ring handle from the return value (`ear = filterPoints(ear);`, `outerNode = filterPoints(outerNode, ...)`), so the return value determines downstream traversal start points and therefore triangle emission order.
- earcut.js has an extra leading `if (!start) return start;`; the C++ header omits it (callers never pass null). Adding it is behavior-preserving for all reachable call sites.
- Unchanged across 2.0.x–2.2.4 and earcut.js 3.0. Very old (1.x) versions had a different signature/loop and no steiner flag.
functions.signature: typename Earcut<N>::Node* Earcut<N>::filterPoints(Node* start, Node* end = nullptr)

functions.name: insertNode
functions.notes: Inserts the new node immediately AFTER `last` (between last and last->next) and returns the NEW node — so linkedList's `last = insertNode(...)` walk builds the ring in input order and leaves `last` at the final vertex. With last == nullptr the node becomes a self-loop (prev = next = itself). Pointer assignment order in the non-null branch is exactly: p->next, p->prev, last->next->prev, last->next — the third statement must read last->next BEFORE the fourth overwrites it. z, prevZ, nextZ, steiner keep their default-member-initializer values (0, nullptr, nullptr, false). The index is narrowed to N via static_cast at construction.
functions.signature: template <typename Point> typename Earcut<N>::Node* Earcut<N>::insertNode(std::size_t i, const Point& pt, Node* last)

functions.name: removeNode
functions.notes: Unlinks from BOTH doubly-linked lists: the polygon ring (prev/next) and the z-order list (prevZ/nextZ). Statement order: ring first (p->next->prev = p->prev, then p->prev->next = p->next), then the two z-guards in the order prevZ, then nextZ. Each z unlink is guarded by a null check because the z list is a plain non-circular doubly-linked list with null ends, and because prevZ/nextZ are null entirely when hashing is off (indexCurve never ran). CRITICAL: removeNode does NOT clear p->prev, p->next, p->prevZ or p->nextZ, and does NOT free the node — the removed node keeps dangling-but-valid pointers into the ring and earcut relies on this (filterPoints reads p->prev right after removing p; cureLocalIntersections/splitEarcut and the isEarHashed z-walk can also still touch removed nodes). Do not add cleanup. The node stays alive in the ObjectPool until the pool is reset.
functions.signature: void Earcut<N>::removeNode(Node* p)

functions.name: splitPolygon (list surgery, included for completeness)
functions.notes: Creates TWO duplicate nodes: a2 (copy of a) and b2 (copy of b), constructed in that order, a2 first, each carrying the SAME index i as its original. This is precisely why every neighbour/exclusion test in this subsystem compares ->i rather than pointers. `an = a->next` and `bp = b->prev` are captured BEFORE any relinking. Eight pointer writes in exactly the order shown. Returns b2 (the copy of b that lands in the second/new ring). The new nodes get z=0, prevZ=nextZ=nullptr, steiner=false, so a split ring is not in the z-index and callers that were hashing must re-run indexCurve on the pieces (earcutLinked does, via its pass logic).
functions.signature: typename Earcut<N>::Node* Earcut<N>::splitPolygon(Node* a, Node* b)

functions.name: eliminateHole / eliminateHoles
functions.signature: Node* eliminateHole(Node* hole, Node* outerNode);  template<typename Polygon> Node* eliminateHoles(const Polygon& points, Node* outerNode);
functions.notes: RANK 1 — most likely to change output on N overlapping squares. With N overlapping squares every hole is bridged into an outer ring that already contains all previously merged holes, so a single divergence here cascades: totally different triangle set and count from the very first hole. functions.name: isValidDiagonal
functions.signature: bool isValidDiagonal(Node* a, Node* b);
functions.notes: RANK 2. Both the "opposite-facing sectors" conjunct AND the zero-length special case are CONFIRMED present in the reference. Exact area expressions recovered: at 0x4044c6, (a->x - a->prev->x)*(b->prev->y - a->y) is subtracted from (a->y - a->prev->y)*(b->prev->x - a->x); at 0x404516, (b->prev->y - a->y)*(b->x - b->prev->x) minus (b->prev->x - a->x)*(b->y - b->prev->y). functions.name: intersects / onSegment / sign
functions.signature: bool intersects(const Node* p1, const Node* q1, const Node* p2, const Node* q2);  bool onSegment(const Node* p, const Node* q, const Node* r);  int sign(double val);
functions.notes: RANK 3. CONFIRMED Variant B. Axis-aligned overlapping squares produce collinear and endpoint-touching segment pairs constantly. intersects() drives (a) cureLocalIntersections' decision to emit a triangle and delete two nodes, and (b) intersectsPolygon's rejection of split diagonals. functions.name: findHoleBridge (first loop: the `if (x == hx) return m` early return)
functions.signature: Node* findHoleBridge(Node* hole, Node* outerNode);
functions.notes: RANK 4 — and this one is very likely responsible for the odd/even-n split visible in the reference outputs. CONFIRMED present: at 0x403de3 `ucomisd %xmm0,%xmm3` (x vs hx) then `je 0x40416a`, and 0x40416a sets the bridge to m and jumps straight to the splitPolygon block, bypassing the second loop entirely. Versions: added in the 2.2.x line as the "hole touches outer ring at a vertex" fix; absent in 2.0.x and early 2.1.x. Observable impact on N overlapping squares: hole i's leftmost point is exactly (2i, 2i) and the accumulating outer ring carries vertical edges at x = 0, n, 2j and 2j+n for every already-merged hole j. x == hx therefore becomes reachable whenever 2j + n == 2i, i.e. whenever n is EVEN. That parity dependence is exactly what the ground-truth sweep shows: odd n (7,9,15,19,21,23,25) all produce the shape `1 2 3 <a> <b> <c> 0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 3` while even n produce a different, longer shape. Getting this early return wrong will flip half of all test values. Also note two sub-details in the same loop that are easy to botch: the guard triple is `hy <= p->y && hy >= p->next->y && p->next->y != p->y` (note `<=` then `>=`), and the endpoint pick is `p->x < p->next->x ? p : p->next` (strict `<`, ties go to p->next).

The getLeftmost y tie-break happens to be a no-op for THIS specific input (holes are inserted in reverse ring order, so the smaller-y of the two leftmost vertices, (2i,2i), is already the traversal start and wins either way) — but it is not a no-op in general, so implement it. functions.name: isEar / isEarHashed (triangle-bbox fast rejects, pointInTriangle variant)
functions.signature: bool isEar(Node* ear);  bool isEarHashed(Node* ear);  bool pointInTriangle(double ax,double ay,double bx,double by,double cx,double cy,double px,double py);
functions.notes: RANK 6 (rank 6 for correctness of the hashed path; the bbox question itself is rank ~12 because it is semantically neutral). CONFIRMED: isEar at 0x4045de goes from the area(a,b,c) reject straight to `p = ear->next->next` with no coordinate bbox compare. isEarHashed at 0x40255d-0x402604 builds all four min/max values and calls zOrder twice (minZ into r12d first at 0x402631, maxZ into eax second at 0x402647); loop guards are `jle` on maxZ forward and `jge` on minZ backward. Important: a pure bbox membership pre-test is CONSERVATIVE — anything outside the triangle bbox is outside the triangle — so adding or omitting it cannot change output for finite coordinates. It is therefore safe either way, and NOT a real risk for this input. What IS output-affecting is JS 3.0's pointInTriangleExceptFirst, which excludes the case p coincides exactly with vertex a; on N overlapping squares many vertices coincide exactly, so a 3.0-based reimplementation would emit a different index stream. Implement the plain pointInTriangle. Versions: 2.0.x-2.2.4 as shown; 3.0 (JS, Nov 2024) changed both. No 3.x release of the C++ earcut.hpp exists as far as I know — v2.2.4 is the last tag.

functions.name: zOrder + operator() hashing setup (inv_size multiply vs size divide, 32767 constant, threshold=80)
functions.signature: int32_t zOrder(const double x_, const double y_);  template<typename Polygon> void operator()(const Polygon& points);
functions.notes: RANK 7 (only bites at n >= 21 for this input). CONFIRMED Variant B: 0x4022e0 is `subsd minX; mulsd inv_size` — one multiply, no divide. The constant at .rodata 0x4050a8 is 0x40DFFFC000000000 = exactly 32767.0 as a double, used as `32767.0 / size` at 0x404d00. The `32767 vs 32767.0` distinction is a non-issue in C++ (integer literal / double still promotes), but VARIANT A vs B is a REAL numeric difference: A rounds twice ((32767*d)/s), B rounds once (d*(32767/s)), so int32 truncation can land on a different bucket, reordering the z-curve and hence isEarHashed's search window. threshold: the literal 80 is CONFIRMED (`mov $0x50,%ebx` at 0x404909) and `hashing = threshold < 0` (`shr $0x1f` sign-bit extract at 0x4049b9). This is the C++ port's reformulation of JS's `data.length > 80 * dim`; both mean "more than 80 total vertices". I am not aware of 80 ever being a different number, nor of a different metric, in the 2.x line. For the squares input each ring has 4 points and there are n rings, so hashing turns on at exactly n >= 21 — the ground-truth sweep confirms output stays well-formed across that boundary (n=20 vs n=21 continue the same parity pattern). REFUTED candidate: `filterPoints` on the outer ring before earcutLinked does NOT exist here — after linkedList(points[0], true) the only guard is `outerNode->prev == outerNode->next`, then eliminateHoles, then earcutLinked. (The genuine historical relative of that candidate is the caller-loop filterPoints inside eliminateHoles; see entry 1.)

functions.name: earcutLinked (pass structure, ear advance, index push order)
functions.signature: void earcutLinked(Node* ear, int pass);
functions.notes: RANK 8 — structurally critical but I found NO version variance in 2.x, so it is a low RISK of divergence, high risk of transcription error. Verified against the binary: loop guard is `ear->prev != ear->next` (0x40458c); prev/next are latched BEFORE the ear test; on success BOTH `ear` and `stop` are reset to next->next (0x4047a9/0x4047b7); the pass dispatch is exactly if(!pass)/else if(pass==1)/else if(pass==2) with GCC turning the tail recursion into a jump back to the loop head with pass bumped to 1 or 2 (so the `if (!pass && hashing) indexCurve` is correctly skipped on re-entry). REFUTED candidate: 'any change in the order the three indices are pushed' — it is prev->i, ear->i, next->i in earcutLinked (0x40470e/0x404735/0x404756) and a->i, p->i, b->i in cureLocalIntersections, in both the reference and every 2.x version I can recall. The only related historical wrinkle is representational, not ordinal: the JS library pushes `node.i / dim | 0` while the C++ port stores the vertex index directly. One reference-specific quirk worth knowing: this build's Node packs `i` into 31 bits with `steiner` in bit 31, so every index read is masked `& 0x7fffffff` — irrelevant for indices below 2^31, but it is why the disassembly shows the mask.

functions.name: cureLocalIntersections
functions.signature: Node* cureLocalIntersections(Node* start);
functions.notes: RANK 9. CONFIRMED Variant B at 0x402a60: short-circuit order is exactly !equals(a,b) -> intersects(a,p,p->next,b) -> locallyInside(a,b) -> locallyInside(b,a); argument order of intersects is (a, p, p->next, b) — note the FIRST argument is a=p->prev, not p. GCC returns filterPoints(start, nullptr) rather than filterPoints(p, nullptr), which is equivalent because loop exit implies p == start. This function runs on pass 1 for the overlapping-squares input, so getting the four-way short-circuit and the (a,p,p->next,b) argument order right matters. It is ranked below intersects itself because the dominant risk here is inheriting the wrong intersects().

functions.name: linkedList / insertNode / splitPolygon / filterPoints (ring construction and mutation)
functions.signature: template<typename Ring> Node* linkedList(const Ring& points, bool clockwise);  Node* splitPolygon(Node* a, Node* b);  Node* filterPoints(Node* start, Node* end);
functions.notes: RANK 10 — no version variance I can identify inside 2.x for splitPolygon/filterPoints, but linkedList determines the vertex NUMBERING and the starting node, so an error here shifts every emitted index. Worked example validating the whole reconstruction, for n=1: ring [(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)] gives sum = +2, so clockwise(true) == (sum>0)(true) => FORWARD insertion, nodes 0..3, and linkedList returns node 3. earcutLinked starts at ear=3: area(2,3,0) = -1 < 0, the only candidate p=1 fails pointInTriangle term 1 (-1 >= 0 false), so ear 3 is cut => emit 2,3,0; then ear = next->next = 1, prev=0 next=2, p == a immediately => emit 0,1,2. Total "2 3 0 0 1 2" — exactly the stated expected output. For holes clockwise=false so `false == true` is false => REVERSED insertion, i.e. hole ring i is linked as (2i,2i+n) -> (2i+n,2i+n) -> (2i+n,2i) -> (2i,2i) with linkedList returning the node for (2i,2i). Two low-rank historical items live here: the trailing-duplicate removal `if (last && equals(last, last->next))` and the `if (list == list->next) list->steiner = true;` degenerate-hole marking in eliminateHoles were both added during the 2.1.x/2.2.x line; both are no-ops for the squares input (rings are 4 distinct unclosed points), so they cannot change these outputs, but implement them anyway.

functions.notes: RANK 12 for this specific input (but rank ~3 for polygons in general). CONFIRMED plain-x: the inlined libstdc++ __insertion_sort at 0x401c70 loads only offset 0 of each Node and does a single comisd — no y load, no slope division anywhere in the sort path. Versions: `a->x < b->x` throughout earcut.hpp 2.0.0-2.2.4 and JS 2.x; compareXYSlope is a JS 3.0 addition. result.determinismNotes:
GROUND TRUTH AVAILABLE ON DISK. /workspace/dataset/test4_executable is an unstripped -O2 GCC 12.1.0 binary of the exact reference. Every claim above was read out of its machine code rather than recalled, and the reconstruction was validated by hand-simulating n=1 to "2 3 0 0 1 2". Verified reference outputs (use these as a test oracle): n=1 "2 3 0 0 1 2"; n=2 "0 1 7 5 3 0"; n=3 "0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 2 0 2 3"; n=4 "5 4 0 0 1 11 7 12 15 13 12 5 0 4 7 3 0 11"; n=5 "9 8 0 0 4 7 1 2 3 0 8 11 3 0 7 5 4 0 0 1 3"; n=6 "9 8 4 0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 15 7 16 19 17 16 5 3 0 15 0 8 11 11 20 23 21 20 9 9 4 0"; n=7 "1 2 3 13 12 8 0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 3"; n=8 "13 12 8 0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 19 7 20 23 21 20 5 3 0 19"; n=20 "37 36 32 0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 43 7 44 47 45 44 5 3 0 43"; n=21 "1 2 3 41 40 36 0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 3"; n=40 "77 76 72 0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 83 7 84 87 85 84 5 3 0 83".

STRUCTURAL OBSERVATION worth exploiting: outputs bifurcate by the parity of n. Odd n >= 7 all collapse to the 15-index form "1 2 3 <a> <b> <c> 0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 3"; even n >= 8 all give the 21-index form "<a> <b> <c> 0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 <d> 7 <d+1> <d+4> <d+2> <d+1> 5 3 0 <d>". Small n (1..6) are irregular. This parity split is almost certainly driven by findHoleBridge's `if (x == hx) return m` early return, which becomes reachable only when a previously-merged hole's right edge at x = 2j + n coincides with the current hole's leftmost x = 2i — i.e. only when n is even. That makes that early return the single highest-leverage detail after the eliminateHole return-value form.

FLOATING-POINT / ORDERING HAZARDS for a byte-exact port:
1. std::sort is NOT stable. The hole queue is sorted with `a->x < b->x` only. If two holes share a leftmost x, the surviving order is libstdc++-introsort-specific. In this build, __introsort_loop is skipped entirely for <= 16 elements and __final_insertion_sort (stable in effect) handles the rest, so <= 16 holes reproduce a stable order; above 16 holes the introsort partitioning can permute equal keys. For the squares input all hole x values are distinct, so this is latent, not active — but do not "fix" it by using std::stable_sort, and do not add a y tie-break to the comparator.
2. Do not algebraically rearrange. area(p,q,r) must stay literally (q->y - p->y) * (r->x - q->x) - (q->x - p->x) * (r->y - q->y). findHoleBridge's ray x must stay p->x + (hy - p->y) * (p->next->x - p->x) / (p->next->y - p->y) — multiply, then divide, then add. middleInside's crossing must stay (p->next->x - p->x) * (py - p->y) / (p->next->y - p->y) + p->x. zOrder must be (v - min) * inv_size, one multiply, never (32767 * (v - min)) / size.
3. inv_size = 32767.0 / std::max<double>(maxX - minX, maxY - minY), guarded by `!= 0.0`, and it is computed AFTER eliminateHoles over the fully bridged ring, not over the input points.
4. qx starts at -std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity() and tanMin at +infinity (both verified as literal inf bit patterns in .rodata, not DBL_MAX).
5. All three pointInTriangle terms use >=. isEar/isEarHashed reject with `area(a,b,c) >= 0` and with `area(p->prev,p,p->next) >= 0`. filterPoints uses `area(...) == 0`. isValidDiagonal's zero-length clause uses strict `> 0`. sectorContainsSector uses strict `< 0` twice. Getting any single one of these backwards changes output on axis-aligned input, where exact zeros are everywhere.
6. Compile with default FP settings. Do not enable -ffast-math or -ffp-contract=fast; the reference was built without FMA contraction (every area is a separate mulsd/mulsd/subsd), and contracting them would change the sign of exactly-zero determinants.

REFERENCE-SPECIFIC NON-SEMANTIC DETAIL: this build's Node is repacked relative to stock earcut.hpp — layout is x@0x00, y@0x08, prev@0x10, next@0x18, z@0x20, then a 32-bit word at 0x24 holding `i` in bits 0..30 and `steiner` in bit 31, then prevZ@0x28, nextZ@0x30 (56 bytes). Hence the `and $0x7fffffff` on every index read and the `orb $0x80,0x27` for steiner=true. This affects nothing observable below 2^31 vertices; mentioned only so the parent is not confused by the masks, and so nobody tries to match stock earcut.hpp line numbers (the assert in indexCurve reports ../earcut.hpp:593, which is shifted by the repack).
